items.html:
By far the most important way to recognize Switzerland, is that all car coverage is low-cam. This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries. This can be recognized in two ways:

  • The car blur is significantly bigger.
  • Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle.

Generally, the bigger car blur is the most consistent way to recognize low-cam.

NOTE: The only other countries that always have low-cam are Japan and Liechtenstein.

Swiss licence plates differ substantially from other European plates. They are fully white and lack the blue strip found in most other European countries.

Front plates are extremely short compared to most in Europe.

Rear plates can be either long or tall. In both cases the red country emblem can be seen on the left, while the canton emblem can be seen on the right.

Swiss bollards are black-and-white with white or grey reflectors. They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.

NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical round bollards.

The colour of directional signs indicates which type of road you are on. Main road signs will be blue, while side roads are white.

Major place names will frequently appear on blue signs, while smaller places tend to be on white signs. However, you can still find large city names on a white sign.

Swiss pedestrian signs have seven stripes, making it almost unique for Europe. Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles.

NOTE: Liechtenstein uses identical signs.

Long dashed yellow road lines are a good clue for Switzerland.

NOTE: These road lines are also common in Liechtenstein.
Pedestrian crossings are typically painted yellow and exclusive to Switzerland and Liechtenstein within Europe.

Swiss road signs commonly have a round, grey metal border around them.

NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical directional signs. Somewhat similar metal borders are found on some directional signs in Denmark.

Town entry signs in Switzerland are usually white or blue, with a metal frame around them.

NOTE: On the back of these signs you may often find the distance to larger, nearby cities. Furthermore, the abbreviation for the canton can often be seen on the bottom of the sign, especially when the town is situated near a canton border.

Chevrons are black with a white arrow. You may also rarely find chevrons that are white with a black arrow.

NOTE: Austrian chevrons are red and white, or red and yellow.

While the southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, with long, thin valleys between the mountains, the northern half mostly consists of large farmlands on either flat ground or rolling hills, typically with forested hills in the distance.

Swiss and Alpine architecture in general largely consists of stone buildings painted in light and warm colours, often combined with wooden parts and details. Roofs are typically tiled and of a gable type. It is extremely common for windows to have wooden shutters which open horizontally in two parts.
These bus stop signs, with thick metal signposts going around them, are unique to Switzerland.

Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh, which are spoken in the regions shown. Note that some areas, mostly near the region borders, are bilingual.

NOTE: Unlike Germany and Austria, Swiss German does not use the letter ß.
The text on the speed limit signs varies depending on the official languages in the region.

Cantons are the first-level administrative division of Switzerland. It is very common to find the two-letter abbreviation for the canton that you are in, as seen on some town entry signs. As such, remembering these can be a great asset when region-guessing Switzerland.

NOTE: If you happen to come across an unblurred licence plate, the first two letters will correspond to the canton that it is registered in.
The first digits of Swiss postal codes are a good way to regionguess the country. The general pattern is that the numbers increase from the west to east.
Elevation is an important part of region-guessing Switzerland. The southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, while the northern half mostly has smaller mountains and hills.
A fairly flat landscape with a long chain of medium-sized, forested mountains northwest means you are likely south of the Jura Mountains.
Exposed limestone rocks, protruding from forested hills, are commonly found in the Jura mountains.
Rock walls are mainly found in the Jura mountains, but can also be found in the Alps, particularly in the Italian speaking parts.

Not unexpectedly, seeing typical Italian architecture in Switzerland should imply that you are in the Italian-speaking areas in the south, principally the canton of Ticino.

The architectural style is characterized by, typically very smooth, orange-yellow stone walls with multiple floors and orange or brownish tiled roofs. Green and brown Italian-style window shutters are common.
Large houses with thick roofs, which are shaped like an arch underneath, are common around Bern.

Elaborate timber frames, which are commonly painted red, are found in the northeast.

NOTE: Simpler timber frames in other colours can be found in other parts of the country.

Around Appenzell, most houses will consist of a large living house connected to a long barn, such that the roof of the living house and the barn are at a 90° angle.

The front facade of the living house will often be divided into small squares, with each window being perfectly contained within a square.
In the canton of Graubünden, you will often come across houses entirely made of stone, with, most commonly white, decorative painted details around windows and the edges of the house.
These large town entry signs can sometimes be found in the canton of Vaud.
Olive green infrastructure, particularly signposts, sign borders and sign backs, are found in Basel-Landschaft.
In the canton of Valais, you will often see thick wooden bollards, which can either be square-shaped or cylindrical.
In place of bollards, reflectors in the canton of Glarus will often be attached to fences following the road.

In Geneva and in the valley between Martigny and Lake Geneva, you can find bike path symbols painted on the road with a simplified person on top of two disconnected wheels.

NOTE: This stands in contrast to the rest of the country, where the symbol will be a somewhat detailed bike.

You may find several different types of road dividers across the country, distributed as seen in this graphic.

_This image was provided by quarksauce. You can click on the image to enlarge it._

If the area around your location appears hilly, but not mountainous, and you manage to catch a glimpse of a large lake to the south, with tall mountains on the other side, then you are very likely north of Lake Geneva.

Seeing a wide lake to the northeast, situated in a landscape with relatively low elevation, means you should be looking at Lake Constance (on some Maps labelled as the Bodensee).

NOTE: Due to the low-lying landscape, you will probably be fairly close to the shore if you see the lake.

The valley of Martigny has the highest density of fruit plantations in the country. It can easily be recognized by the many small fruit trees in combination with the wide, flat valley with large mountains on either side.
Apart from the valley of Martigny, the most likely area to find fruit trees is near Lake Constance, followed by the area northwest of Lake Geneva.

In the canton of Graubünden, you can find this unique and easily recognizable train coverage on the tracks of the “Bernina Express.” It runs around most of the canton, all the way down to Tirano in Italy.

Generation 2 coverage is very limited in Switzerland. It can be found mostly near the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais, and on a few very short stretches in Schaffhausen.

NOTE: This does not include the many ski resorts with Generation 2 snow coverage, which can be found throughout the southern half of the country.
These blue street signs, with rounded edges on the sides, are unique to the city of Sankt Gallen.
Large blue street signs, attached to a low double signpost, similar to directional signs in Denmark, are found in Basel.
Downtown Bern can be recognized by this specific architecture. Grey toned buildings, typically with four floors and large, somewhat rounded openings lined up on the ground floor are common.

GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends you play these maps instead:

  • Switzerland - Schweiz - Suisse - Svizzera - Svizra (map link) - 6k+ handpicked pinpointable locations.
  • IntersectionGuessr - Switzerland (map link) - 20k arbitrarily generated locations at intersections, and therefore potentially pinpointable (but this is not guaranteed).
  • Lakes of Switzerland - Schweizer Seen - Lacs Suisses (map link) - Map for practising lakes in Switzerland. Locations are not necessarily pinpointable.

lm.name: Romansh
lm.note:
Romansh is a language spoken in parts of western Switzerland. You will often find it mixed in with German (and possibly Italian). Most helpful may be to learn a few words that you may see and recognize that if you are in Switzerland but it's not one of the other 3 languages it's Romansh.

  • ospidal - hospital
  • scoula - school
  • bainvgnieu - welcome
  • limita generala - speed limit
  • restorant - restaurant
  • parc naziunal - national park
  • svizzer - switzerland
  • attenziun - warning

lm.name: Appenzell Architecture
lm.note: Around Appenzell, houses often have a living area joined to a long barn at a 90° angle. The front of the house is usually divided into neat squares, each containing a window.

lm.name: Arch Roofs
lm.note: Large houses with thick roofs, which are shaped like an arch underneath, are common around Bern.

lm.name: Basel Street Signs
lm.note: Large blue street signs, attached to a low double signpost, similar to directional signs in Denmark, are found in Basel.

lm.name: Cycling Paints
lm.note:
In Geneva and in the valley between Martigny and Lake Geneva, you can find bike path symbols painted on the road with a simplified person on top of two disconnected wheels.

NOTE: This stands in contrast to the rest of the country, where the symbol will be a somewhat detailed bike.

lm.name: Fruit PLantations
lm.note: The Martigny valley has the highest density of fruit plantations in Switzerland. It's easy to spot by its many small fruit trees and the wide, flat valley between tall mountains.

lm.name: Glarus Bollards
lm.note: In place of bollards, reflectors in the canton of Glarus will often be attached to fences following the road.

lm.name: Italian architecture
lm.note: If you see Italian-style architecture in Switzerland, you're likely in the south, mainly in Ticino. Buildings often have smooth orange-yellow walls, tiled roofs, and green or brown shutters.

lm.name: Lake Geneva
lm.note: If you're in a hilly area and see a large lake to the south with high mountains beyond, you're likely just north of Lake Geneva.

lm.name: Lake of Constance
lm.note: A wide lake to the northeast in low-lying terrain likely means you're seeing Lake Constance (also called the Bodensee).

lm.name: Limestone Rocks
lm.note: Exposed limestone rocks, protruding from forested hills, are commonly found in the Jura mountains.

lm.name: Rock Walls
lm.note: Rock walls are mainly found in the Jura mountains, but can also be found in the Alps, particularly in the Italian speaking parts.

lm.name: St. Gallen Street Signs
lm.note: These blue street signs, with rounded edges on the sides, are unique to the city of Sankt Gallen.

lm.name: Stone Houses
lm.note: In the canton of Graubünden, you will often come across houses entirely made of stone, with, most commonly white, decorative painted details around windows and the edges of the house.

lm.name: Timber Frames
lm.note:
Elaborate timber frames, which are commonly painted red, are found in the northeast.

NOTE: Simpler timber frames in other colours can be found in other parts of the country.

lm.name: Town Entry Signs
lm.note: These large town entry signs can sometimes be found in the canton of Vaud.

lm.name: Train Coverage
lm.note: In Graubünden, the “Bernina Express” was used for a distinctive and easily recognizable train coverage that runs through much of the canton and down to Tirano in Italy.

lm.name: Valais Bollards
lm.note: In the canton of Valais, you will often see thick wooden bollards, which can either be square-shaped or cylindrical.

lm.name: Barns - Ticino Huts
lm.note: Huts in Ticino often have stone as their primary building material, with their roofs often made from slate tiles.

lm.name: Roof Features - Low-Pitched Roofs
lm.note: Wide houses with strikingly low-pitched roofs and often a large number of windows are frequently found in the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel, as well as in the northern part of the canton of Bern. A variant with a half-hipped roof also exists.

lm.name: Barns - Attached Barns
lm.note: Barns in Appenzell and the surrounding area are often directly attached to the main house in a T-shaped or L-shaped layout, making them often easy to recognise from a distance.

lm.name: Barns - Barn Lofts
lm.note: These upper-floor wooden balconies are commonly seen on barns in southwestern Valais.

lm.name: Barns - Bulky Barns
lm.note:
In the canton of Bern, the design of barns generally mirrors the local architecture. Barns in this region are typically bulky in appearance and frequently have half-hipped roofs. The roofs may also feature timber supports.

A variant exists with an additional entrance for vehicle access. Sometimes the barn will be directly attached to the house.

lm.name: Barns - Corner Barns
lm.note: Barns featuring a combination of wood and either concrete or stone can be found in Valais and Grisons. Typically, the concrete or stone elements are located at the corners of the barns. As with huts, exposed round beams are only found in Grisons.

lm.name: Barns - Cyborg House-Barns
lm.note: In the Entlebuch region, in the far south of the canton of Lucerne, you can find ‘cyborg’ house-barns with the house and barn ‘fused’ together. These buildings are particularly striking when viewed from the front.

lm.name: Barns - Flap-Roof Barns
lm.note: Like houses in the same region, barns in the area shown on the map can sometimes have double-pitched gable roofs, with the lower part of the roof at a shallower angle.

lm.name: Barns - Grisons Huts
lm.note: A key feature of huts in Grisons is the frequent use of round beams, rather than rectangular ones, either for the overall structure or just in the gable area. Huts with just rectangular beams can still be seen in this area.

lm.name: Barns - Low-Pitched Roofs
lm.note:
Barns in the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel often have low-pitched roofs, mirroring the design of local houses.

The barns often form part of the same building as the main house, although can be separate. Either version may feature large double doors for vehicle access.

lm.name: Barns - Raccards
lm.note: Raccards are the traditional raised wooden granaries of Valais. They are generally built on short stilts with a round stone slab on each stilt to guard against rodents.

lm.name: Barns - Tent-Roof Barns
lm.note: Strikingly wide barns with tent-like roofs, resembling those found on houses in the region, can be found in the northern half of the canton of Bern.A variant of these barns exists with an additional covered entrance allowing vehicle access.

lm.name: Barns - Tiled-Gable Barns
lm.note:
In western Fribourg, you can find barns with gables that are clad with either terracotta-coloured tiles or occasionally grey, diamond-shaped ones.

A variant of these barns also exists with an additional entrance for vehicle access.

lm.name: Barns - Traverse Roof Barns
lm.note: In **Zug **and neighbouring cantons, you can find barns with a prominent transverse roof extending below the main gable.

lm.name: Barns - Undulating Gable Arches
lm.note:
Similar to houses in the region, barns in the canton of Lucerne can feature an undulating gable arch, or, unlike the houses, a semicircular gable arch.

Barns in this area may also have a distinctive style of half-hipped roof with a tiny triangular gable.

Variants of these barns exist with an entrance for vehicle access.

lm.name: Barns - Valais Huts
lm.note: The walls of wooden huts in Valais are often made from a system of interlocking rectangular logs, easily visible from the outside of the building.

lm.name: Barns - X-Barns
lm.note: This diamond lattice pattern on the doors of barns is found in the cantons of Thurgau and Zurich.

lm.name: Churches - Multi-Spire Churches
lm.note: Church towers featuring multiple small spires surrounding a main spire are most common in the west of the country, particularly around Neuchâtel, although they can occasionally be seen elsewhere

lm.name: Churches - Multi-Triangle Gable Churches
lm.note: Church towers where the tower walls form triangular gables, pointing up, on multiple sides, occur most frequently in the northeast.

lm.name: Churches - Onion-Dome Churches
lm.note: Churches with onion domes are a strong indicator for the non-French-speaking regions of Switzerland, although exceptions exist elsewhere.

lm.name: Churches - Onion-Shaped Clock Churches
lm.note: Church towers featuring an onion-shaped gable structure around a clock face can be found in a central band from the canton of Bern in the west to Glarus in the east.

lm.name: Churches - Rooster Church Steeples
lm.note: A rooster on top of a church steeple usually signifies a Protestant church and is a strong indicator for the French-speaking part of the country, although isolated examples can be found elsewhere.

lm.name: Churches - Simple Triangular Gable Churches
lm.note: Church towers with a simple triangular gable shape are most frequently found in northern and central Switzerland.

lm.name: Religious Shrines -Ticino Cappellittas
lm.note: Catholic shrines in Ticino will often be colourful and feature religious imagery. Shrines in this area may also have slate roofs.

lm.name: Roof Features - Balcony Gables
lm.note: In the canton of Neuchâtel, these wide houses with low-pitched roofs will sometimes have a balcony integrated into the gable. You will also sometimes see wood-clad gable arches on these houses.

lm.name: Roof Features - Bump Finials
lm.note: Finials in the form of a small bump on a roof can be found in the areas shown on the map, being common in the cantons of Vaud, Fribourg, Geneva and Neuchatel and also in western Valais. They can also very rarely be found in the canton of Bern.

lm.name: Roof Features - Diamond-Shaped Slates
lm.note: Roofs featuring large, diamond-shaped, slate slabs are found across central Valais.

lm.name: Roof Features - Downward Pointing Finials
lm.note: Downward-pointing finials at the ends of the load-bearing beams on gable roofs can be found in the areas shown on the map. They can take a variety of shapes, ranging from rectangular to ornamental forms.

lm.name: Roof Features - Flap Roofs
lm.note: Double-pitched gable roofs, with the lower part of the roof at a shallower angle, can be seen in the area shown on the map.

lm.name: Roof Features - Front Chimneys
lm.note: Chimneys located on the small gable roof of ​​half-hipped roofs or very close to the gable on hipped roofs are particularly found in western Switzerland, especially in the cantons of Vaud and Fribourg, although exceptions can rarely be found elsewhere.

lm.name: Roof Features - Gable-End Chimneys
lm.note: In the valleys of central Ticino, you will find houses with gable-end chimneys.

lm.name: Roof Features - Metal Panel Roofs
lm.note: In Valais and Grisons, rectangular metal panels are sometimes used to roof houses and sheds. They are particularly found in the northwest of Grisons.

lm.name: Roof Features - Slate Roofs
lm.note: Slate roofs are commonly found in the three southern cantons of Valais, Ticino, and Grisons.

lm.name: Roof Features - Tent Roofs
lm.note: Strikingly wide houses resembling tents, with deeply overhanging roofs and a bulky overall appearance, can be found in the northern half of the canton of Bern.

lm.name: Roof Features - Thick Arched Gables
lm.note: In the canton of Bern and neighbouring cantons, houses featuring half-hipped roofs with a thick arch under the gable, giving the house a bulky appearance, can be found.

lm.name: Roof Features - Ticino Slates
lm.note: In Ticino, slate roofs will sometimes be organised in neat rows of slate tiles, as opposed to the less regular pattern normal on other slate-roofed houses in Switzerland.

lm.name: Roof Features - Tiled House Gables
lm.note: Houses with gables covered with striking red tiles are frequently found in northeastern Vaud and the west of the canton of Fribourg. In exceptional cases, similar tiled gables can be found outside these regions however.

lm.name: Roof Features - Undulating Gable Arches
lm.note: Gables in the canton of Lucerne commonly have arches similar to those you see in the canton of Bern. However unlike the simple semicircular arches in Bern, the arches are undulating.

lm.name: Roof Features - Valsot Flat Roofs
lm.note: Most houses in Valsot, in the extreme east of the country, have very flat roofs with a barely noticeable slope. These houses can also be found in other nearby villages.

lm.name: Wall Features - Arched Gates
lm.note: Houses with arched gates can be found in the north and west of the country as shown on the map. Traditionally serving as entrances to farmhouses and barns, they now often conceal modern apartments, shops or restaurants.

lm.name: Wall Features - Colorful Shingle Wall Cladding
lm.note: Shingle walls in a range of pastel colours are found primarily in the east of the country, becoming less common towards the west, although can be occasionally found anywhere. The shape of shingles can vary: round, rectangular, diamond and cone shapes all exist.

lm.name: Wall Features - Decorative Carvings
lm.note:
Dark-wood houses that are particularly wide can be seen in the southern parts of the cantons of Bern and Vaud and in northwestern Valais.

Common features of these houses include:

  • wood carvings and inscriptions with the year of construction or other text
  • decorative soffits can along the edge of the roof
  • either a staircase or a pair of staircases
  • covered balconies and verandas on the side of the house.

You can also see timber versions of the thick arched roofs common in this area.

lm.name: Wall Features - Devant Huis
lm.note: A devant-huis is a traditional, wide, recessed entranceway of a building found in the canton of Jura. There will often be vertical timber plank cladding above the entrance.

lm.name: Wall Features - Light Colored Mortar
lm.note: Buildings with walls made of irregular stones plastered with a thick, light-coloured mortar, often smeared over the stones, are found in Valais, Ticino and the Italian-speaking parts of Grisons.

lm.name: Wall Features - Pale Yellow Bricks
lm.note: Pale yellow bricks are found in a broad strip stretching from Bern in the west to St. Gallen in the east. Buildings can be entirely constructed from these bricks. However, you can also often see the bricks used in conjunction with decorative red bricks and in otherwise wooden buildings.

lm.name: Wall Features - Rectangular Panel Houses
lm.note:
A very distinctive style of house is found in the Appenzell cantons and neighbouring St. Gallen.

These houses have rows of sets of shutterless windows on the gable side of the house, with rectangular panels underneath and between the sets of windows.

A ‘baroque’ variant of this style can be found, commonly in urban settings, with a distinctive curved roof shape and often decoration on the panels.

lm.name: Wall Features - Sgraffito
lm.note: In Grisons, you will find the traditional decorative technique known as sgraffito, where intricate patterns or motifs are carved into the fresh, light lime plaster of house facades to reveal the darker layer of plaster beneath.

lm.name: Wall Features - Sgraffito Val Müstair
lm.note: Val Müstair, in the far east of Grisons, paints its houses with a unique variant of Grisons sgraffito with more colours and a different style of designs. Normal sgraffito can also be found here

lm.name: Wall Features - Structural Curve Houses
lm.note: In Obwalden and surrounding areas, you can find dark-wood houses (in varying styles) with a structural curve along the length of a wall supporting a cantilevered upper storey. This upper storey sometimes includes a balcony.

lm.name: Wall Features - Subtle Window Roofs
lm.note: Houses with ‘miniature roofs' over windows are found in the area shown on the map. Sometimes these ‘miniature roofs' will span the whole wall and sometimes just the windows below them.

lm.name: Wall Features - Tall & Narrow Houses
lm.note:
Dark-wood houses in the mountainous north-south valleys of Valais are comparatively tall and narrow.

Often roofed with slate tiles, these houses frequently feature multiple balconies and decorative wooden fretwork. Interlocking log joints, a typical feature of the region, are usually visible at the corners of the houses.

lm.name: Wall Features - Timber & White-Plastered Walls
lm.note: Houses blending timber and white-plastered walls are most common in Valais and northern Grisons, typically following a one-third to two-thirds ratio of either material.

lm.name: Wall Features - Timber Frame Houses East
lm.note:
Timber frame houses are found in two main regions of Switzerland as shown on the map. There are rare exceptions elsewhere.

In the northeastern distribution area, common features of timber frame houses include double-pitched gable roofs and large dormers. Additionally these houses can sometimes take the form of long buildings running lengthwise along the street.

lm.name: Wall Features - Timber Frame Houses West
lm.note:
Timber frame houses are found in two main regions of Switzerland as shown on the map. There are rare exceptions elsewhere.

In the western distribution area, you will often see timber frame houses with thick arched gables, triangular timber supports under the roof, and large tent roofs.

lm.name: Wall Features - Window Roofs
lm.note: Houses featuring multiple small roofs on the gable end can be found in the areas shown on the map, although can exceptionally be found elsewhere. The small roofs will sometimes also continue along the side walls of the building.

lm.name: Wall Features - Wooden Shingle Wall Cladding
lm.note: Traditional wooden shingle wall cladding is found across a central belt stretching from the canton of St. Gallen in the east to Valais in the west. The shapes of the shingles can vary and may be rounded or angular.

lm.name: Switzerlans - Roof Features - Slate Finials
lm.note: In the southernmost parts of Valais, notably around Zermatt and Evolène, you can sometimes find slate roofs featuring slate finials above the gables.

lm.name: Low cam
lm.note:
All the coverage in Switzerland is taken with a low-cam. The only other two countries with low-cam are Japan and Sri Lanka, but they look different.

You can recognize low-cam by the wide blur of the Street View car and the lower vantage point compared to the normal camera.

lm.name: French
lm.note:
Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. French is the second most spoken language in Switzerland after German. It is spoken in western parts of the country. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.

NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

lm.name: German
lm.note:
Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. German is the most widely spoken language in Switzerland. It is (mostly) spoken in central and northern parts of the country. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.

NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

ALSO NOTE: Unlike Germany and Austria, Swiss German does not use the letter ß, replacing it by ss in words like Straße (street), becoming Strasse in Swiss German.

lm.name: Italian
lm.note:
Switzerland has four official languages spoken in their own regions of the country. Italian is spoken in southern parts of the country, close to Italy. You can often use place names on the map to tell what language is spoken where.

NOTE: Some areas, mostly near language borders, are bilingual.

lm.name: bus stop signs
lm.note: These bus stop signs, with thick metal signposts going around them, are unique to Switzerland.

lm.name: Basel street sign
lm.note: Large blue street signs, attached to a low double signpost, similar to directional signs in Denmark, are found in Basel.

lm.name: Geneva street sign
lm.note:
If you know your in Switzerland and you see these dark blue street signs with Rue written on it, The only city that has these is Geneva.

NOTE: This design can commonly be found in France so make sure to confirm your in switzerland.

lm.name: Zurich street sign
lm.note: Zurich street signs are blue with a white edge and 4 thick dots in each corner.

top.html:
By far the most important way to recognize Switzerland, is that all car coverage is low-cam. This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries. This can be recognized in two ways:

  • The car blur is significantly bigger.
  • Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle.

Generally, the bigger car blur is the most consistent way to recognize low-cam.

NOTE: The only other countries that always have low-cam are Japan and Liechtenstein.
top.raw: By far the most important way to recognize Switzerland, is that all car coverage is **low-cam**. This means that the camera on the Google car is intentionally set up lower than in most other countries. This can be recognized in two ways: - The car blur is significantly bigger. - Roads look wider and objects around you are seen from a lower angle. Generally, the bigger car blur is the most consistent way to recognize low-cam. NOTE: The only other countries that always have low-cam are [Japan](https://www.google.com/maps/@35.8415638,139.9145236,3a,75y,305.11h,83.84t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sLyYnyrI7fgLeL5Ev09XeJg!2e0!6shttps:%2F%2Fstreetviewpixels-pa.googleapis.com%2Fv1%2Fthumbnail%3Fpanoid%3DLyYnyrI7fgLeL5Ev09XeJg%26cb_client%3Dmaps_sv.tactile.gps%26w%3D203%26h%3D100%26yaw%3D33.088177%26pitch%3D0%26thumbfov%3D100!7i16384!8i8192) and [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/jn7cXhtXQRG6Hd9a6).

top.html:
Swiss licence plates differ substantially from other European plates. They are fully white and lack the blue strip found in most other European countries.

Front plates are extremely short compared to most in Europe.

Rear plates can be either long or tall. In both cases the red country emblem can be seen on the left, while the canton emblem can be seen on the right.
top.raw: Swiss **licence plates** differ substantially from other European plates. They are fully white and lack the blue strip found in most other European countries. **Front plates** are extremely short compared to most in Europe. **Rear plates** can be either long or tall. In both cases the red country emblem can be seen on the left, while the canton emblem can be seen on the right.

top.html:
Swiss bollards are black-and-white with white or grey reflectors. They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top.

NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical round bollards.
top.raw: Swiss bollards are **black-and-white **with white or grey reflectors. They can be either wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top. NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical [round bollards](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JJSg67HrDHerzv8c7).

top.html:
The colour of directional signs indicates which type of road you are on. Main road signs will be blue, while side roads are white.

Major place names will frequently appear on blue signs, while smaller places tend to be on white signs. However, you can still find large city names on a white sign.
top.raw: The colour of **directional signs** indicates which type of road you are on. Main road signs will be blue, while side roads are white. Major place names will frequently appear on blue signs, while smaller places tend to be on white signs. However, you can still find large city names on a [white sign](https://goo.gl/maps/pfJ2QNrPFmB7q6xN9).

top.html:
Swiss pedestrian signs have seven stripes, making it almost unique for Europe. Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles.

NOTE: Liechtenstein uses identical signs.
top.raw: Swiss pedestrian signs have **seven stripes**, making it almost unique for Europe. Furthermore, rather than the typical European square shape, the signs appear as tall blue rectangles. NOTE: Liechtenstein uses identical signs.

top.html:
Long dashed yellow road lines are a good clue for Switzerland.

NOTE: These road lines are also common in Liechtenstein.
top.raw: **Long dashed yellow** road lines are a good clue for Switzerland. NOTE: These road lines are also common in Liechtenstein.

top.html: Pedestrian crossings are typically painted yellow and exclusive to Switzerland and Liechtenstein within Europe.
top.raw: Pedestrian crossings are typically painted **yellow** and exclusive to Switzerland and [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/WLYNNkZAGCz7rDLg8) within Europe.

top.html:
Swiss road signs commonly have a round, grey metal border around them.

NOTE: Liechtenstein uses almost identical directional signs. Somewhat similar metal borders are found on some directional signs in Denmark.
top.raw: Swiss road signs commonly have a round, grey **metal border** around them. NOTE: [Liechtenstein](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wbSfjB8xPexuUkqZA) uses almost identical directional signs. Somewhat similar metal borders are found on some directional signs in [Denmark](https://goo.gl/maps/gQWu5BCRsga8WkiS7).

top.html:
Town entry signs in Switzerland are usually white or blue, with a metal frame around them.

NOTE: On the back of these signs you may often find the distance to larger, nearby cities. Furthermore, the abbreviation for the canton can often be seen on the bottom of the sign, especially when the town is situated near a canton border.
top.raw: Town entry signs in Switzerland are usually **white or blue**, with a **metal frame** around them. NOTE: On the back of these signs you may often find the distance to larger, nearby cities. Furthermore, the abbreviation for the canton can often be seen on the bottom of the sign, especially when the town is situated near a canton border.

top.html:
Chevrons are black with a white arrow. You may also rarely find chevrons that are white with a black arrow.

NOTE: Austrian chevrons are red and white, or red and yellow.
top.raw: **Chevrons** are black with a white arrow. You may also rarely find chevrons that are [white with a black arrow](https://goo.gl/maps/S8YmmUW2vnbEQryN9). NOTE: Austrian chevrons are red and white, or red and yellow.

top.html: While the southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, with long, thin valleys between the mountains, the northern half mostly consists of large farmlands on either flat ground or rolling hills, typically with forested hills in the distance.
top.raw: While the southern half of Switzerland is extremely mountainous, with long, thin valleys between the mountains, the northern half mostly consists of large farmlands on either flat ground or rolling hills, typically with forested hills in the distance.

top.html: Swiss and Alpine architecture in general largely consists of stone buildings painted in light and warm colours, often combined with wooden parts and details. Roofs are typically tiled and of a gable type. It is extremely common for windows to have wooden shutters which open horizontally in two parts.

Roofs are typically tiled and of a gable type. It is extremely common for windows to have wooden shutters which open horizontally in two parts.
